analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators permanently ban energy market manipulators from electricity and gas trading.
analysis.headline: A bill giving the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission power to bar manipulators from electricity and natural gas markets was introduced with two Democratic senators' support and has seen no committee action since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill lets the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) ban, temporarily or permanently, any person or company caught manipulating electricity markets or filing false information about natural gas prices from buying and selling energy or transmission services. It also creates a new federal prohibition on knowingly filing false natural gas price data with government or private price-reporting agencies. The goal is to protect households and businesses from price spikes caused by rigged energy markets.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that pay electricity and natural gas bills. When traders manipulate energy markets, the inflated costs flow through to utility bills; this bill aims to raise the personal and corporate price of getting caught, by barring bad actors from the market entirely.

how_it_helps.text: The bill authorizes FERC to prohibit, conditionally or unconditionally, temporarily or permanently, any person who has manipulated electricity markets from buying or selling electric energy, electricity products including financial transmission rights, or transmission services [S3].

It creates a new Natural Gas Act provision making it illegal to willfully and knowingly file false information with federal or private-sector price-reporting agencies about the availability, prices, transportation, or sale of natural gas [S3].

It gives FERC matching ban authority over natural gas: anyone who violates the market-manipulation or false-reporting rules can be barred from buying or selling natural gas or transmission services [S3].
The changes extend ban authority from 'individuals' to any 'person,' covering companies and other entities acting directly or indirectly, and close gaps in existing enforcement provisions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Energy trading firms, merchant power companies, and natural gas sellers that manipulate markets or report false price data would face exclusion from the market — the bill's intended cost. Legitimate market participants also face the risk of FERC exercising its new ban authority, which trades some certainty for stronger deterrence.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on FERC to detect and prove manipulation after the fact; banning bad actors after prices have already spiked compensates no one for the inflated bills they paid in the meantime [S3].

Granting FERC authority to bar any 'person' from trading, conditionally or unconditionally and for any period the Commission determines, concentrates significant discretionary power in regulators; market participants and some lawmakers argue broad ban authority can chill legitimate trading activity [S3].
The bill does not set price limits, require refunds to customers harmed by manipulation, or change how manipulation cases are investigated — it only adds a penalty tool to existing enforcement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, targeted enforcement upgrade: it does not cap prices or restructure markets, it just adds a lifetime-ban stick to FERC's existing tools for electricity and gas market manipulation. The cost falls almost entirely on actors who violate manipulation rules, plus some added regulator discretion. The main honest limitation is that deterrence after the fact does little for customers who already paid manipulated prices, and the bill does nothing to speed up detection or refunds.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which has taken no further action on it, so it currently has no path to a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the bill on April 21, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S5].
Senator Maria Cantwell joined as a cosponsor; the bill has one cosponsor, both Democrats [S4].
No further action — no hearings, markup, or floor vote — has been recorded since the referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has gone nowhere, energy traders and gas sellers face no new ban risk or false-reporting liability, and FERC has no new enforcement tool to use against market manipulation.

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.role: U.S. Senator from Nevada; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Energy Consumer Protection Act of 2026 and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since April 2026.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor are Democrats, and no Republicans have signed on; with Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats and controlling the committee, the bill has no visible path forward.

industries.industry: Energy trading firms and merchant power companies
industries.note: Firms that manipulate electricity markets or file false gas price data could be permanently barred from buying or selling energy and transmission services. Manipulated energy prices flow directly into household and business utility bills, so the industry's gain from lax enforcement comes at consumers' expense.

The bill creates a new criminal-adjacent prohibition on knowingly filing false price and availability data with federal or private price-reporting agencies, on top of ban authority for violators. Honest sellers are unaffected; the burden falls on those who game reported prices, which ripple through gas bills.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican-controlled Senate and no Republican cosponsors, a bill referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee with no action after introduction will in most cases die quietly at the end of the Congress. Absent a hearing or markup being scheduled, the realistic path is that it never reaches the floor.
